lesson.title: Cut, Splice, Repeat: Inside the Spliceosome
lesson.summary: Before a pre-mRNA can leave the nucleus, a large molecular machine called the spliceosome cuts out interrupting sequences and joins the remaining pieces back together into one continuous coding message.
lesson.body:
A gene in eukaryotic DNA is not transcribed as one uninterrupted coding sequence. The pre-mRNA that comes off the DNA template, the same pre-mRNA that just received its cap and tail as part of mRNA processing, contains stretches that will be kept and stretches that must be removed before the message means anything to a ribosome. Splicing is the process that does the removing, and it has to be done with single-nucleotide precision, because even one base out of place would throw off the reading frame for everything downstream of it.

The machine that performs this editing is called the spliceosome, a large complex built from several small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles, each one a combination of RNA and protein, that assemble onto the pre-mRNA at the boundaries between the sequences to be removed and the sequences to be kept. Those boundaries are marked by short, highly conserved signal sequences: the sequence to be removed almost always begins with GU and ends with AG, a pattern often remembered as the GU-AG rule. Once the spliceosome components are in place, splicing proceeds through two linked chemical reactions. In the first, a specific adenine nucleotide located near the far end of the removable sequence reaches around and attacks the boundary at the near end, folding that sequence into a loop, called a lariat because of its rope-like shape, and freeing the upstream piece that will be kept. In the second reaction, the free end of that upstream piece attacks the boundary at the far end, joining the two flanking pieces directly together and releasing the looped, unwanted sequence entirely.

Why go through all this rather than simply transcribing a clean, uninterrupted gene in the first place? Part of the answer is that interrupted genes give the cell flexibility, since which sequences get kept does not have to be fixed, a point that becomes central once we get to alternative splicing. But whatever the deeper evolutionary reasons, the immediate requirement is precision: the removed sequences are generally not a multiple of three nucleotides and would scramble the reading frame if left in, so accurate, reproducible cutting and rejoining is what converts a raw transcript into a message a ribosome can actually translate correctly.
